WHAT: Pixel sampling reveals glass compositor permanently tints key backgrounds
WHERE: KeyboardView.swift applyColors()
HOW:
  Native letter keys: #FFFFFF (255,255,255)
  Our letter keys: #E2E4E8 (226,228,232) — Δ29 across all channels
  Native special keys: #FFFFFF (also white!)
  Our special keys (after fix): #FFFFFF — matches native
  Keyboard background: #E2E4E8 — both match perfectly

WHY: Native iOS keyboard and our extension both use letterKeyColor = UIColor(white: 1.0, alpha: 1.0). The glass compositor in the extension host tints the key backgrounds to partially blend with the backdrop. This is iOS compositor behavior we can't override.

GOTCHA: Δ29 is visible if you're pixel-peeping but imperceptible in normal use. Attempting to compensate (setting alpha higher) doesn't work — the compositor always applies the tint. Special keys (shift, delete, 123, emoji, return) should also be set to white — they match native exactly once set to UIColor(white: 1.0, alpha: 1.0).

KEY FINDING: On native iOS, ALL keys (letter AND special) use the SAME color (#FFFFFF). The visual distinction between key types comes from icon style (filled vs outlined shift arrow), not background color.
